generatedDescriptions.description: Your stomach drops before your mind catches up — a visceral lurch, like the floor tilting, the moment you sense a fracture forming between people. Your attention snaps to the gap: the person sitting slightly outside the circle, the silence that landed wrong, the tension no one else seems to notice yet. Time compresses into a narrowing window where the crack is still small enough to close, and everything in you leans toward the space between them, your hands almost restless with the pull to weave the torn edges back together before the fraying sets.

A lightness rises through your chest and into your feet, as though the ground has tilted gently forward and you're already partway to moving. Your attention catches on edges — the turn in the corridor you haven't taken, the unfamiliar voice in the next room — and the present moment widens around them, unhurried but open, the way a doorway feels when you notice it's been left ajar. There's warmth in it, not the scalding kind but steady, the quiet certainty that whatever is on the other side of the threshold will be worth the crossing.

A prickling warmth spreads across your fingertips and up through your palms, as if something just out of reach is pulling at the nerve endings — your chest opens slightly, breath shallow not from anxiety but from a leaning-forward alertness that narrows the world to whatever seam or edge has caught your notice. Time thickens and stretches the way an afternoon can vanish inside an attic, each failed attempt not discouraging but deepening the texture of the problem, and you feel the gravitational pull to turn the thing over one more time, to try the next key, because the weight of the unopened is more vivid than anything already known.

driveCompetition.differentiationText: How they differ: One pull opens the chest and widens the gaze — warmth radiating outward, attention scanning for who is here and what they need, the moment feeling like a current you can step into alongside others. The other pull narrows behind the eyes — a focused tightening, attention locking onto what is hidden or not yet known, time suspending as everything else falls away. One draws you forward into the space between people; the other draws you downward into the thing itself. Notice which one widens your attention toward someone present versus narrows it toward something not yet revealed.

How they differ: One pull opens the chest and lifts the gaze outward — attention widens toward what is unfamiliar or unexplored, the moment feels spacious and unhurried, and the body wants to move toward and into. The other pull tightens in the stomach and draws attention inward to the space between people — scanning for tension, rupture, or someone left outside — and the moment takes on a pressing, time-sensitive quality that pulls toward bridging or mending. Notice which one is doing something to your gut versus your chest, and whether your attention is reaching outward toward the new or scanning inward toward the relational field.

How they differ: One pull brightens and narrows — a tingling aliveness in the fingers and eyes, attention funneling onto something not-yet-known, time stretching open as the body leans forward, drawn to reach, turn over, look closer. The other pull spreads and weighs — a dropping heaviness in the chest and stomach, attention scattering outward to scan the space between people, the moment contracting with urgency as the body braces and orients toward others, drawn to step in, soothe, close a gap. Notice which one narrows your focus forward toward something unopened, and which one widens your awareness sideways toward the people around you.

These are the experiences that made you who you are.

**Age 11:** Your class went on a field trip to a cave. Most children were scared. You walked deeper than anyone else, your heart hammering. You found a crystal formation no one else had seen. You didn't tell anyone about it for a week — you just carried the secret, warm and private.

**Age 7:** Your parents argued at dinner. You felt sick — physically sick, a tightness in your stomach that wouldn't let you eat. The argument went on for what felt like hours. When they finally laughed about something, the tightness dissolved so suddenly it left you dizzy.

**Age 5:** You found a locked box in your grandmother's attic. You spent the whole afternoon trying every key in the house — drawer keys, cupboard keys, the tiny key from your music box. When you finally opened it and found just old letters, the disappointment lasted only a moment.

**Age 9:** A new family moved in next door. You were the first to visit, bringing cookies before your mother told you to. The girl spoke a different language. You communicated in drawings all summer — maps of the neighbourhood, portraits of each other's pets, elaborate treasure hunts. It was the most fun you'd ever had, and you never shared a word.

**Age 13:** Your best friend was being excluded by the popular group. You chose the friend over the group. The popular girls stopped talking to you. Your friend said 'You didn't have to do that.' You said 'I know.'

When people around you are at peace, something in you settles. When they argue, your body knows before your mind — a tightness in your stomach, a wrongness you can feel. You value harmony not as a preference but as a physical need. You reach out to strangers because connection comes naturally. You chose your friend over popularity because the choice was never really close.
You trust easily and feel comfortable with closeness. When someone you care about is near, you feel settled.
